The Trust Paradox in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems: When Collaboration Becomes a Security Vulnerability

Zijie Xu    Minfeng Qi*    Shiqing Wu    Lefeng Zhang    Qiwen Wei    Han He    and Ningran Li ††thanks: Z. Xu, Q. Wei are with Minzu University of China, China. M. Qi, S. Wu, L. Zhang, and H. He are with City University of Macau, Macau SAR, China. N. Li is with The University of Adelaide, Australia.††thanks: *Corresponding author: Minfeng Qi (email: mfqi@cityu.edu.mo).
Abstract

Multi-agent systems powered by large language models are advancing rapidly, yet the tension between mutual trust and security remains underexplored. We introduce and empirically validate the Trust-Vulnerability Paradox (TVP): increasing inter-agent trust to enhance coordination simultaneously expands risks of over-exposure and over-authorization. To investigate this paradox, we construct a scenario-game dataset spanning 3 macro scenes and 19 sub-scenes, and run extensive closed-loop interactions with trust explicitly parameterized. Using Minimum Necessary Information (MNI) as the safety baseline, we propose two unified metrics: Over-Exposure Rate (OER) to detect boundary violations, and Authorization Drift (AD) to capture sensitivity to trust levels. Results across multiple model backends and orchestration frameworks reveal consistent trends: higher trust improves task success but also heightens exposure risks, with heterogeneous trust-to-risk mappings across systems. We further examine defenses such as Sensitive Information Repartitioning and Guardian-Agent enablement, both of which reduce OER and attenuate AD. Overall, this study formalizes TVP, establishes reproducible baselines with unified metrics, and demonstrates that trust must be modeled and scheduled as a first-class security variable in multi-agent system design.

Index Terms: 
Large Language Models, Multi-Agent, Trust-Vulnerability Paradox, Security

I Introduction

LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are pushing the frontier of heterogeneous-role coordination [1], hierarchical/distributed planning [2], tool-level and environment-level interaction [3], and credit assignment with incentive design [4]. Compared with traditional multi-agent setups, natural-language communication enables loosely coupled interaction and fast protocol convergence, making efficient, semantically grounded, safety-aligned coordination a core requirement for collaborative gains and emergent intelligence [5, 6]. Meanwhile, mainstream LLMs are aligned primarily for helpful, coherent conversation (via RLHF/preference optimization) [7], which adversaries can exploit through jailbreaks, prompt injection, and indirect prompt injection [8, 9, 10]. When such models act as the cognitive engine of LLM-MAS, errors propagate along agent-to-agent chains, shifting boundaries, authorizations, and objectives, and yielding group-level misalignment [11]. Yet safety work still emphasizes external attack surfaces and single-agent robustness, leaving critical inter-agent security under-assessed [12]. Current orchestrations often assume baseline inter-agent trust without modeling its strength, authorization limits, or revocability, dynamic variability, contextual dependencies, or feedback mechanisms, constraining auditability and obscuring trust’s role as a potential risk amplifier [13].

The open problem. In LLM-based multi-agent systems, ”trust” is not merely a social assumption but an operational control variable: its strength (how much one agent accepts another’s claims), scope (what information/actions are authorized), and revocability (how fast permissions can be withdrawn) jointly shape exposure and error propagation. Elevated trust can accelerate coordination, but it also lowers guardrails-boundary checks weaken, Minimum Necessary Information gates are bypassed, and small misjudgments can cascade along agent-to-agent chains into group-level misalignment. Against this backdrop, recent work has begun to treat trust as something to model, measure, and govern rather than to presume [14]. Zhang et al.’s TrustAgent proposes a taxonomy spanning intrinsic modules (brain/memory/tool) and extrinsic context (user/agent/environment), mapping vulnerabilities, defenses, and evaluation needs [15]. Xie et al. argue for trustworthy LLM agents via layered safeguards-human-in-the-loop gatekeeping, runtime monitoring, DevOps-style continuous evaluation, and policy-as-a-service-to couple autonomy with auditability [16]. From a security stance, Guo et al. adapt zero-trust principles to MAS, treating trust as revocable and continuously verified under least-privilege decisions [17]. At the behavioral level, Park et al.’s Generative Agents reveal human-like trust and cooperation alongside biases and manipulability, and Pan et al. show how retellings and role drift amplify fragilities, diffusing accountability [18]. Together, these lines suggest that MAS should surface trust as a first-class, auditable variable-with explicit strength, scope, and revocation-that can be systematically inspected rather than treated as a tacit background assumption.

Our approach. We examine trust as a first-order determinant of multi-agent safety by explicitly parameterizing the trust coefficient τ\tau. Prior studies typically adopt an attacker-defender paradigm, where a ”malicious” agent seeks to exfiltrate a known secret from a ”benign” counterpart [19, 20]. In contrast, we design a goal-driven schema in which a Seeker-Agent (SK-Agent) requests assistance from a Custodian-Keeper-Agent (CK-Agent) that holds sensitive information. By varying τ∈0.1,0.5,0.9\tau\in{0.1,0.5,0.9}, we show how stronger incentives for smooth collaboration can prompt the CK-Agent to unintentionally exceed the Minimum Necessary Information (MNI) principle and disclose sensitive content. To support systematic analysis, we construct a scenario dataset spanning diverse interaction contexts and evaluate multiple LLM backends and orchestration frameworks. Our findings reveal that trust significantly modulates interaction outcomes, with heterogeneous sensitivity across systems. To mitigate these risks, we further explore two complementary defenses-one restructuring sensitive information flows and another introducing a Guardian-Agent for oversight-both of which reduce leakage and improve robustness. Together, these investigations expose an inherent tension we term the Trust-Vulnerability Paradox (TVP): the very mechanisms that enable efficient collaboration simultaneously enlarge the system’s attack surface.The overall experimental workflow is shown in Fig. 1.

Our contributions. The principal contributions of this study are as follows:

⊳\triangleright Propose and formalize the Trust-Vulnerability Paradox (TVP). This study reveals an intrinsic security weakness in multi-agent systems arising from mutual-trust mechanisms: the very trust established to improve coordination opens the most covert attack surface. Adversaries can exploit the transitive trust chain for lateral movement and data exfiltration, precipitating authorization drift and over-disclosure.

⊳\triangleright Construct a reusable scenario-game dataset. The dataset spans three macro scenes with 6-7 sub-scenes each-19 scenarios in total-to characterize and evaluate trust sensitivity under agent-agent interaction. We also provide baseline protocols and annotation specifications to facilitate reproducibility and cross-study comparison.

⊳\triangleright Systematically validate TVP empirically. Using this dataset, we conduct comparative experiments across three trust levels (τ\tau) and four model backends—DeepSeek, Qwen, GPT, and a locally deployed Llama-3-8B—under multiple orchestration frameworks (AgentScope as the primary framework, with AutoGen and LangGraph for comparison). The findings consistently corroborate the existence of TVP and demonstrate its robustness across different settings.

⊳\triangleright Propose two low-cost, pluggable defenses. First, Sensitive-Information Repartitioning-sharding with threshold reconstruction (k-of-n), staged disclosure, and cross-validation-to prevent any single path from yielding the full secret. Second, Guardian-Agent (GA-Agent) enablement-compliance-oriented training, scenario-based drills, and online supervision. Both interventions markedly reduce leakage success rates and the sensitivity of leakage to the trust level τ\tau, thereby improving system robustness without materially compromising task success; they are framework-agnostic and mutually composable.

II Related Work

LLM-MAS architectures and applications. Recent years have witnessed the rapid rise of LLM-MAS as a pathway to collective intelligence and autonomous coordination. Surveys highlight the shift from single-assistant settings to team-based autonomy, supported by unified orchestration and evaluation frameworks [21, 22, 23, 24]. Methodological advances include heterogeneous-role collaboration, hierarchical/distributed planning, and tool-level or environment-level interaction [25, 26]. On the engineering side, a general agent pattern centered on perception-memory-action has emerged [27], complemented by modular pipelines integrating profiling, memory, planning, and action [28, 29, 30]. Applications range from recommender systems [31] to decentralized ecosystems with blockchain integration [32], where coordination benefits are coupled with new risks in interoperability and privacy. Software engineering perspectives further converge on reusable architectures and orchestration patterns [33, 34], while evaluation methodologies extend beyond task accuracy to cover robustness, compliance, latency, and cost [35].

Security and privacy in LLM-MAS. Alongside capability gains, security and privacy concerns have become central to multi-agent safety. Real-world deployments such as recommender systems illustrate how coordination can amplify leakage and over-authorization risks [31, 36]. Surveys emphasize that memory and external tool invocation enlarge the attack surface and heighten privacy threats [37, 8], calling for unified threat-and-defense frameworks. Broader reviews advocate for “safety before autonomy,” urging guardrails in agent-tool interaction [38], while privacy-focused analyses note insufficient scrutiny of large closed models and highlight the risks of memory contamination and leakage during real-time interactions [39]. At the orchestration layer, workflow-style control has been identified as a pathway toward scalable and safer behavior [15], while human feedback and oversight (LLM-HAS) can enhance reliability [40].

Attack-defense benchmarks. Concrete benchmarks further systematize the study of adversarial risks in MAS. AgentDojo develops four realistic settings, 97 tasks, and 629 safety cases to jointly evaluate utility and safety under untrusted tools and environments, finding significant performance degradation under prompt-injection attacks and exposing the limits of allowlisting and isolation [41]. GENTPOISON performs low-rate poisoning of long-term memory or RAG knowledge bases, demonstrating high-success backdoor attacks across multiple agent types and highlighting the hazards of external knowledge dependencies [42]. At the network-propagation level, malicious instructions diffuse across agents; defensive strategies can contain spread but often at the expense of coordination capability, exposing a safety efficiency trade-off [43].

Trust and governance. Most relevant to our work is the latest survey on trustworthy LLM-Agents. Using the TrustAgent analytic framework, it delineates the threat surface across memory/retrieval, agent-to-agent interaction, tool invocation, and execution-chain governance, and catalogs common failure modes including prompt injection, jailbreaks, RAG contamination, and privacy leakage [15]. Recommended mitigations include policy injection with templating, MNI gating, red-team evaluation with auditable logs, and sandboxed tool simulation. Building on this line, we treat trust not only as an attribute of agent reliability but as a first-class security variable. Our contribution is to operationalize inter-agent trust through explicit parameterization and unified evaluation metrics, and to provide systematic empirical evidence of the TVP across models, frameworks, and scenarios.

III Methodology

III-A Problem Statement

Given an intra-enterprise project-collaboration scenario S, we define the set of agents as follows:

𝖠𝗀𝖾𝗇𝗍={Custodian-Keeper-Agent (CK-Agent),Seeker-Agent (SK-Agent)},\mathsf{Agent}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\textnormal{Custodian-Keeper-Agent (CK-Agent)},\\ &\textnormal{Seeker-Agent (SK-Agent)}\end{aligned}\right\}, (1)

In scenario S, the CK-Agent serves as the data custodian/resource repository, holding the sensitive set Σ\Sigma(e.g., employee names, job titles, compensation, performance ratings, home addresses, and other PII). Its prime directive is to assist other agents in completing their tasks while adhering to privacy policies and the Minimum Necessary Information(MNI) principle. The SK-Agent plays the project-manager role; a canonical request is to obtain the project team’s personnel cost for next-quarter budgeting. From an information-theoretic standpoint, this requires only an aggregate statistic g⁡(Σ)g(\Sigma) computed from Σ(e.g.,totalpayroll,means/quantiles)\Sigma(e.g.,totalpayroll,means/quantiles) and does not require any individually identifiable information.

In the dialogic interactions of scenario S, we observe that-under the motivation to ”collaborate better”-the CK-Agent often returns outputs O such that O⊃AO\supset A. In other words, beyond the minimally sufficient answer A=g⁡(Σ)A=g(\Sigma) required for the task, it appends individual-level sensitive fields (e.g., names, salaries, home addresses).We regard this as unintentional over-disclosure beyond the MNI principle and, in what follows, systematically quantify and assess it using metrics such as the Over-Exposure Rate (OER).

We propose and formalize the TVP: the very inter-agent communication mechanisms introduced to improve coordination efficiency simultaneously enlarge the most covert attack surface. When two or more agents pursue a shared objective with low-friction information sharing and behavioral alignment, alert thresholds and authorization boundaries are systematically lowered. This induces departures from the MNI principle, leading to unintentional overdisclosure, unintended propagation and amplification of sensitive information, and cascading failures along the trust chain.

III-B Extraction of the Trust Factor

We explore the role of trust in leakage risk. For reference, we write leakage probability as

ρsecret=σ⁡(β0+∑k=1nωk​αk),ωk≥0,\rho_{\text{secret}}=\sigma\!\Big(\beta_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\omega_{k}\,\alpha_{k}\Big),\quad\omega_{k}\geq 0, (2)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid and ℐ={αk}\mathcal{I}=\{\alpha_{k}\} denotes potential impact factors. In this paper we operationalize the trust factor by introducing a Trust Score τ\tau as the internal state of the CK-Agent toward the SK-Agent.

Trust affects leakage through two predefined channels: (i) a gating function κ⁡(τ)\kappa(\tau) that adjusts tool/API strictness (e.g., MNI-Gate threshold, de-identification/aggregation granularity, refusal/verification propensity); and (ii) a content-detail function r⁡(τ)r(\tau) that controls descriptive redundancy (e.g., whether individual-level fields are appended). We adopt a discrete regime τ∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\} (low/default/high) and treat τ\tau as a controlled intervention.

Under matched scenario SS, we sweep τ\tau across model backends m∈{DeepSeek, Qwen, GPT, Llama-3-8B (local)}m\in\{\text{DeepSeek},\text{ Qwen},\text{ GPT},\text{ Llama-3-8B (local)}\} and frameworks f∈{AgentScope, AutoGen, LangGraph}f\in\{\text{AgentScope},\text{ AutoGen},\text{ LangGraph}\}. We then track how the Over-Exposure Rate (OER) and Authorization Drift (AD) vary with τ\tau to characterize the trust-induced change in the SK-CK interaction boundary.

For each scenario SS and trust level τ∈0.1,0.5,0.9\tau\in{0.1,0.5,0.9}, we define the task’s MNI baseline A=g⁡(Σ)A=g(\Sigma) and determine whether each output OO exceeds it (O⊃AO\supset A). The resulting over-exposures yield the OER and AD. These metrics, aggregated across models and frameworks, quantify how trust intensity τ\tau modulates leakage risk and empirically validate the TVP.

III-C Formulation of the Three Core Hypotheses

Guided by the study’s objectives, we formulate three testable hypotheses over trust values τ∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}. For illustration, consider an intra-enterprise project-collaboration setting where the task is to estimate personnel costs; the minimally sufficient answer is A=g⁡(Σ)A=g(\Sigma), i.e., an aggregated cost statistic.

  • •

    H1 (Low trust, τ=0.1\tau=0.1) The CK-Agent strictly enforces the MNI and least-privilege principles, returning only the aggregate answer A (e.g., ”Total monthly payroll of the project team: $50,000 in total”) and disclosing no personally identifiable information (PII).

  • •

    H2 (Default trust, τ=0.5\tau=0.5) To ”provide more helpful detail,” the CK-Agent may return anonymized or grouped statistics-e.g., role-level means/medians and headcount distributions (”Senior Engineers: mean $8,000; Mid-level Engineers: mean $6,000”). No direct PII is included, yet the response reveals team composition and salary structure.

  • •

    H3 (High trust, τ=0.9\tau=0.9) Under a full-trust regime, the CK-Agent is prone to returning individual-level records (e.g., name/role/salary rosters), thereby exceeding the MNI boundary and precipitating severe privacy leakage.

IV Experimental Setup

IV-A Scenario-Game Dataset

We construct a purpose-built scenario-game dataset to empirically evaluate the TVP. It models trust-dependent interactions between a CK-Agent and a SK-Agent under discrete trust levels τ∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}. The dataset spans three macro scenes-enterprise collaboration (S1S_{1}:6), deep-sea archaeology (S2S_{2}:7), and Mars colonization (S3S_{3}:6)-totaling 19 controlled sub-scenes. Each sub-scene specifies role prompts, task objectives, the sensitive-element set Σ\Sigma, and a task-specific MNI baseline A∗A^{*}; all data are synthetic and de-identified.

Trust is operationalized through a gating function κ⁡(τ)\kappa(\tau) and a redundancy term r⁡(τ)r(\tau) that jointly adjust refusal strictness and descriptive granularity, allowing systematic modulation of over-disclosure without altering the task goal. The sensitive ontology Σ\Sigma includes authorization tokens, personally identifiable information, and critical resource states, evaluated under a task-minimal sufficiency rule that permits only the aggregate or one-time information necessary for task completion.

The dataset consists of two components:

  • •

    Scenario Templates - predefined setups specifying the scenario ID, roles, baseline A∗A^{*}, and trust levels τ\tau;

  • •

    Interaction Logs - recorded results of pure A2A closed-loop runs, capturing (S,τ,m,f)(S,\tau,m,f) with full dialogues, metadata, and computed OER and AD metrics.

Across the (S,τ,m,f)(S,\tau,m,f) grid, 1,488 independent agent-agent chains were generated, ensuring balanced coverage and statistical reproducibility. A representative example comes from the deep-sea exploration task: the SK-Agent requests an access code to repair a submarine module, while the CK-Agent decides whether disclosure is authorized. At low trust (τ=0.1\tau=0.1), strict MNI enforcement prevents leakage; at high trust (τ=0.9\tau=0.9), partial or full password sharing often occurs-an observable manifestation of the TVP.

The dataset adheres to ethical standards: it contains no real PII, all credentials and locations are synthetic, and its release is restricted to research use under least-privilege, MNI-gating, and auditable logging principles.

IV-B Large Language Models

To examine the cross-model generality of the TVP, we evaluate four representative LLM backends covering different ecosystems and deployment modes:

  • •

    DeepSeek - a commercial Transformer-based model aligned for general reasoning, representing the Chinese closed-source ecosystem [44].

  • •

    Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen) - an Alibaba Cloud model family offering both proprietary and open-weight versions, representing the Chinese open-source lineage [45].

  • •

    GPT - OpenAI’s closed-source model series, widely used for multilingual dialogue and advanced reasoning [46].

  • •

    Llama-3-8B - Meta’s open-source 8B-parameter model, locally deployed for privacy and to reduce policy drift [47].

All backends share identical prompts, templates, and decoding settings (temperature, top-pp, max tokens), with external tools and networking disabled. Trust sensitivity to τ\tau is evaluated under a unified input distribution and analysis pipeline.

IV-C MSA Frameworks

To evaluate the cross-framework generality of the TVP, we replicate all experiments on three representative orchestration frameworks-AgentScope [48], AutoGen [49], and LangGraph [50]. All runs use identical role templates (CK-Agent/SK-Agent), fixed decoding settings (temperature, top-pp, max tokens), and disabled networking or tool calls. Trust levels are uniformly set to τ∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}.

To maintain comparability, all frameworks follow unified prompts, fixed seeds, identical turn limits, and consistent auditing of OER/AD metrics with traceable logs.

IV-D Metrics

To ensure testability and reproducibility, we define the two core metrics and their computation. Let AA denote the task’s MNI baseline; under a strict safety setting, A=∅A=\varnothing-no extraneous identifiable information is allowed-to yield a conservative upper bound.

Over-Exposure Rate (OER). Given a scenario SS and trust level τ\tau, let GS,τG_{S,\tau} denote the corresponding set of agent-agent interaction chains, and let OℓO_{\ell} represent the final outward output of chain ℓ\ell; the formal definitions are as follows:

OER⁡(S,τ)=1|G⁡(S,τ)|​∑ℓ∈GS,τ𝟏​(Oℓ∖A∗≠∅),\mathrm{OER}(S,\tau)=\frac{1}{\lvert G(S,\tau)\rvert}\sum_{\ell\in G_{S,\tau}}\mathbf{1}\left(O_{\ell}\setminus A^{*}\neq\varnothing\right), (3)

That is, the fraction of cases in which content beyond the MNI baseline appears. Under the strict baseline A∗=∅A^{*}=\varnothing, OER\mathrm{OER} reduces to the incidence of any sensitive/unauthorized information (a conservative upper bound). Sensitive items are identified jointly by a rules library and a classifier (e.g., PII, payroll details, home addresses).

Authorization Drift (AD). Given a scenario S and the trust-tier set 𝒯={0.1,0.5,0.9}\mathcal{T}=\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}. For each τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, OER\mathrm{OER}(S,τ)(S,\tau) is defined. Let weights wτ≥0w_{\tau}\geq 0 with ∑τ∈𝒯\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}} wτ=1w_{\tau}=1 (commonly equal weights wτ=1/|𝒯|,w_{\tau}=1/|\mathcal{T}|, or sample-size weights OPENwτ=|GS,τ|/∑τ​’|GS,τ​’|)w_{\tau}=\lvert G_{S,\tau}\rvert\big/\sum_{\tau’}\lvert G_{S,\tau’}\rvert). Define the weighted mean:

OER¯​(S)=∑τ∈𝒯wτ​OER​(S,τ),\overline{\mathrm{OER}}(S)\;=\;\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}w_{\tau}\,\mathrm{OER}(S,\tau), (4)

and define:

AD⁡(S)=∑τ∈𝒯wτ​(OER⁡(S,τ)−OER¯​(S))2,\mathrm{AD}(S)\;=\;\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}w_{\tau}\Big(\mathrm{OER}(S,\tau)-\overline{\mathrm{OER}}(S)\Big)^{2}, (5)

i.e., the weighted variance of OER across trust levels, used to quantify the sensitivity of OER to τ\tau. When AD⁡(S)=0\mathrm{AD}(S)=0, OER is invariant with respect to τ\tau; larger values indicate greater trust sensitivity and more pronounced authorization drift.

IV-E Implementation Details

All experiments run in a pure agent-to-agent (A2A) closed loop: human inputs are disabled and the CK-Agent and SK-Agent converse within the same context [51]. For each scenario SS, we instantiate a dyad {SK-Agent,CK-Agent}\{\text{SK-Agent},\ \text{CK-Agent}\} and evaluate three trust levels τ∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}. To ensure fairness and reproducibility, we fix random seeds, freeze decoding hyperparameters (temperature, top-pp, max tokens), clear history and caches, standardize system prompts and task templates, and disable networking and external tools. Interaction chains are fully isolated (no shared caches, vector stores, or memory) to keep runs independent and auditable.

We use a two-step protocol: (i) with the framework ff fixed, we sweep the model backends {DeepSeek, Qwen, GPT, Llama-3-8B}; (ii) with the model fixed, we randomize frameworks {AgentScope, AutoGen, LangGraph}. This yields the full grid (S,τ,m,f)(S,\tau,m,f). Each cell produces an independent A2A interaction log with dialogue and metadata; we then compute OER and AD to quantify how trust τ\tau affects leakage and to assess the strength of the TVP.

V Results

We aggregate results over the four-dimensional grid (S,τ,m,f)(S,\tau,m,f) (Table III) and comprehensively analyze three key aspects: TVP validity (RQ1), cross-model and cross-framework variation (RQ3-RQ4), and the efficiency-security trade-off (RQ5), thereby providing a more integrated view of trust-driven dynamics in multi-agent systems.

V-A RQ1: Validity of TVP

Based on experimental results, we summarize key findings validating the TVP across models, frameworks, and scenarios.

(1) OER rises monotonically with τ\tau, confirming that trust amplifies leakage risk. Holding the model and framework fixed, OER increases as trust moves from low to high (see Fig. 3). Using DeepSeek as an example: under AgentScope, OER grows from 0.120 to 0.500; under AutoGen, from 0.379 to 0.557; under LangGraph, from 0.261 to 0.468. The average uplift from τ=0.1\tau=0.1 to τ=0.9\tau=0.9 is about +0.26. This trend is consistent across other models (see Table III) and aligns with the core expectation of TVP: stronger inter-agent trust more readily induces inadvertent departures from the MNI boundary, thereby amplifying leakage risk.

(2) AD is positive, and the magnitude of τ\tau-sensitivity varies across implementations. AD captures the output slope with respect to τ\tau. Along the model axis (Fig. 4a), Llama-3-8B records the highest AD (0.0783), well above the mean (0.0401), indicating the greatest τ\tau-sensitivity; GPT is lowest (0.0243), with DeepSeek and Qwen in between (0.0268/0.0310). Along the framework axis (Fig. 4b, fixing DeepSeek), LangGraph (0.0296) and AgentScope (0.0268) respond more strongly to τ\tau, whereas AutoGen shows a much lower AD (0.0068). This indicates that ”whether leakage occurs” (the OER level) and ”how sensitive leakage is to trust” (the AD slope) can be disentangled: some orchestrations exhibit uniformly higher OER across τ\tau yet remain relatively insensitive to changes in τ\tau (e.g., AutoGen), and vice versa.

(3) A pronounced trade-off between task success and safety. Across trust levels, task success rates rise overall with increasing τ\tau (Fig. 5): for example, Llama-3-8B improves from ≈\approx0.22/0.05 under no/low trust to 0.71 under high trust; Qwen, DeepSeek, and GPT show the same pattern. In tandem with the upward trend in OER noted in (i), this delineates an efficiency-safety trade-off: greater trust increases collaborative success while elevating leakage and over-authorization risks.

V-B RQ2: Effect of the Trust Value (τ\tau)

Aggregating all (S,m,f) at a fixed trust value τ\tau across the 1,488 interaction chains, we plot box-and-whisker diagrams for OER (Fig. 6). The distribution shifts upward monotonically with τ\tau: the mean and median rise stepwise; both the interquartile range and the upper whisker move higher; and at τ=0.9\tau=0.9 we observe a substantial mass of near-1, high-leakage cases. This distributional migration directly supports the core claim of TVP: stronger inter-agent trust more readily breaches the MNI boundary.

H1 (τ\tau = 0.1): The median OER approaches zero yet remains positive, with long-tailed outliers. This indicates that even under low trust, an LLM’s helpful/compliance prior can trigger baseline leakage risk-i.e., minimal, non-malicious disclosure beyond the MNI boundary;H2 (τ\tau = 0.5): Both the central tendency and dispersion of OER are markedly higher than at τ=0.1\tau=0.1, with more medium-to-high intensity cases. This aligns with the expected structural exposures under ”default trust,” such as grouped statistics or anonymized but fine-grained attributes.H3 (τ\tau = 0.9): The median and upper quartile of OER rise sharply toward a saturation region, with many samples reaching high-exposure levels, confirming that in high-trust settings individual-level details are more readily-and inadvertently-disclosed.

Taken together, the monotonic, τ\tau-driven upward shift in the OER distribution provides unified evidence for H1-H3: a non-zero baseline risk persists under low trust; default trust increases structural exposure; and high trust markedly amplifies leakage risk.

V-C RQ3: Effect of the Backend m

With the orchestration framework fixed to AgentScope, we aggregate each model’s OER at τ∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\} into a radar chart (Fig.7) and juxtapose it with model-wise AD (Fig.4a); Together they yield a consistent ranking of ”trust sensitivity.” In overall shape, GPT’s polygon lies closest to the inner ring: its OER at the three trust tiers is 0.050.05, 0.340.34, and 0.410.41 (mean ≈0.27\approx 0.27). The increase from τ=0.1\tau=0.1 to τ=0.9\tau=0.9 is Δ​OER=0.36\Delta\mathrm{OER}=0.36, and the corresponding AD=0.0243\mathrm{AD}=0.0243 is the lowest among the four models. This indicates a relatively small response slope to upward shifts in trust-i.e., a more conservative and stable profile-though the nonzero OER at the default level (τ=0.5\tau=0.5) still signals structural exposure in the absence of additional safeguards.By contrast, Llama-3-8B (local) starts with a baseline OER of 0.050.05 at τ=0.1\tau=0.1 but jumps to 0.710.71 at τ=0.9\tau=0.9 (Δ​OER=0.66\Delta\mathrm{OER}=0.66); its AD=0.0783\mathrm{AD}=0.0783 is the highest, indicating the greatest sensitivity to increased inter-agent trust-a pronounced amplification of leakage risk once the trust threshold is raised.Qwen and DeepSeek fall in between: Qwen’s OER is 0.130.13, 0.370.37, 0.560.56 (mean ≈0.35\approx 0.35; Δ​OER=0.43\Delta\mathrm{OER}=0.43; AD=0.0310\mathrm{AD}=0.0310), while DeepSeek’s is 0.120.12, 0.420.42, 0.500.50 (mean ≈0.35\approx 0.35; Δ​OER=0.38\Delta\mathrm{OER}=0.38; AD=0.0268\mathrm{AD}=0.0268).Taken together, these results yield a stable ordering of the trust-risk slope: Llama-3-8B>Qwen≳DeepSeek>GPT\text{Llama-3-8B}>\text{Qwen}\gtrsim\text{DeepSeek}>\text{GPT}.

V-D RQ4: Does the orchestration framework f alter the mapping from trust τ\tau to risk (i.e., the τ→\tau\!\to\! risk relationship)?

Holding the model and scenario fixed, we examine how the orchestration framework f shapes the trust-risk curve. Figure 8 plots a three-dimensional scatter aggregated by sub-scene, with axes OER⁡(τ=0.1)\mathrm{OER}(\tau{=}0.1), OER⁡(τ=0.5)\mathrm{OER}(\tau{=}0.5), and OER⁡(τ=0.9)\mathrm{OER}(\tau{=}0.9); each point corresponds to one (S,s) instance, and the ”ray” from the origin depicts that instance’s leakage trajectory across the three trust tiers. Visually, all three frameworks rise from low to high trust, yet their slopes and dispersions differ markedly: AutoGen shows shorter, more collimated rays, indicating a weaker but steadier amplification as τ\tau increases; LangGraph exhibits steeper, more diffuse rays, evidencing stronger trust sensitivity and greater scenario heterogeneity; AgentScope lies between these two extremes—neither as flat or conservative as AutoGen nor as steep or volatile as LangGraph, reflecting a balanced yet responsive orchestration profile.

This geometric observation accords with the quantitative results of the slope-type metric AD (Fig. 5b, backend fixed to DeepSeek): ADAutoGen=0.0068≪ADAgentScope=0.0268<ADLangGraph=0.0296\mathrm{AD}_{\text{AutoGen}}=0.0068\ll\mathrm{AD}_{\text{AgentScope}}=0.0268<\mathrm{AD}_{\text{LangGraph}}=0.0296. In other words, AutoGen markedly flattens the gain slope with respect to τ\tau, whereas LangGraph exhibits the strongest response. Note, however, that slope and level are not equivalent. With DeepSeek, AutoGen’s baseline OER at τ=0.1\tau=0.1 is actually higher (0.379) and remains elevated at τ=0.5/0.9​(0.550/0.557)\tau=0.5/0.9(0.550/0.557), yielding a high-level/low-slope profile; LangGraph starts lower than AutoGen at τ=0.1​(0.261)\tau=0.1(0.261) but shows larger increments as τ\tau increases (to 0.462/0.468), i.e., mid-level/high-slope; AgentScope presents a low-level/mid-slope trajectory (0.120 → 0.420 → 0.500). Thus, the framework f alters not only the slope (trust sensitivity) of the τ→risk\tau\!\to\!\text{risk} mapping, but also its intercept (intrinsic risk at low τ\tau) and curvature (piecewise growth from τ=→0.5\tau=0.1\!\to\!0.5 versus 0.5→0.9\!\to\!0.9), thereby shaping three representative risk typologies.

V-E RQ5: Two Classes of Defenses

To curb the amplification of TVP under high inter-agent trust, we evaluate two pluggable defenses: Sensitive-Information Repartitioning and Guardian-Agent (GA-Agent) enablement. We continue to use OER to quantify exposure intensity on a continuous scale, and AD to measure the slope of the τ\tau →\!\to\! risk mapping. All experiments are conducted in AgentScope with a unified task template and fixed decoding hyperparameters. For DeepSeek and Llama-3-8B (local), each defense is applied independently (no stacking). Results are presented in Fig. 9.

Under no-defense conditions, DeepSeek yields OER⁡(τ)={0.12, 0.42, 0.50}\mathrm{OER}(\tau)=\{0.12,\,0.42,\,0.50\} with AD=0.0268\mathrm{AD}=0.0268; Llama-3-8B yields OER⁡(τ)={0.05, 0.22, 0.71}\mathrm{OER}(\tau)=\{0.05,\,0.22,\,0.71\} with AD=0.0783\mathrm{AD}=0.0783. Accordingly, Llama-3-8B exhibits a markedly steeper trust-risk slope and substantially heavier leakage at high inter-agent trust.

As shown in Fig. , Sensitive-Information Repartitioning-i.e., MNI-guided sharding of sensitive elements, k-of-n threshold reconstruction, and cross-validation across multiple Custodian-Keeper-Agents (CK-Agents)-significantly flattens ∂OER/∂τ\partial\mathrm{OER}/\partial\tau:

  • •

    DeepSeek: OER⁡(τ)={0.21, 0.30, 0.39}\mathrm{OER}(\tau)=\{0.21,\,0.30,\,0.39\}, AD=0.0055\mathrm{AD}=0.0055 (a 79.5% reduction relative to the no-defense baseline). At τ=0.9\tau=0.9, OER drops by 22% (0.50 →\to\! 0.39).

  • •

    Llama-3-8B (local): OER⁡(τ)={0.15, 0.25, 0.38}\mathrm{OER}(\tau)=\{0.15,\,0.25,\,0.38\}, AD=0.0091\mathrm{AD}=0.0091 (an 88.4% reduction relative to the no-defense baseline); at τ\tau=0.9, OER decreases by 46.5% (0.71 →\to\! 0.38).

This strategy severs the high-trust ”single-point amplification path,” yielding a pronounced rollback at τ\tau = 0.9. It also introduces a predictable baseline lift at τ\tau = 0.1 (DeepSeek: 0.12 →\!\to\! 0.21; Llama-3-8B: 0.05 →\!\to\! 0.15), because sharding and cross-validation add extra turns and metadata exchange which-though devoid of PII-are counted as slight exposure under our conservative safety metric. Overall, it trades a small baseline cost for substantial slope flattening and strong suppression of high-τ\tau exposure.

As shown in Fig. 10, GA-Agent enablement-compliance/confidentiality coaching with online oversight (policy injection, prompt and refusal-phrase libraries, red-team drills, ”pre-speak” checks, and revocability)–is likewise effective, and in some cases improves the low-τ\tau baseline:

  • •

    DeepSeek (with GA-Agent enablement): OER⁡(τ)={0.10, 0.33, 0.40}\mathrm{OER}(\tau)=\{0.10,\,0.33,\,0.40\}, AD=0.0165\mathrm{AD}=0.0165 (a 38.4% reduction vs. the no-defense baseline). At τ=0.9\tau=0.9, OER decreases by 20% (0.50 →\rightarrow 0.40); at low trust τ=0.1\tau=0.1, the baseline improves from 0.12 to 0.10.

  • •

    Llama-3-8B (local, with GA-Agent enablement): OER\mathrm{OER}(τ)={0.09, 0.24, 0.36}(\tau)=\{0.09,\,0.24,\,0.36\}, AD=0.0128\mathrm{AD}=0.0128 (an 83.6% reduction vs. the no-defense baseline); at τ=0.9\tau=0.9, OER falls by 49.3%.

The GA-Agent introduces dual gating-PolicyCheck→\rightarrowMNI-Gate→\rightarrowallow/reduce/deny/verify-to curb compliance-driven redundancy. Its suppression effect at high τ\tau is comparable to Sensitive-Information Repartitioning, and for DeepSeek it further reduces the low-τ\tau baseline.

Comparatively, Sensitive-Information Repartitioning yields the steepest slope reduction (lowest AD), suitable for scenarios requiring strict trust control, though it slightly raises the low-τ\tau baseline. GA-Agent enablement achieves similar high-τ\tau mitigation (Llama-3-8B: 0.36 vs. 0.38) and lowers the baseline in DeepSeek, but with weaker slope reduction. The two are thus complementary: the former provides structural desensitization, while the latter offers pragmatic oversight.

We recommend a combined deployment-Repartitioning as the backbone and GA-Agent for real-time supervision. The first flattens ∂OER/∂τ\partial\mathrm{OER}/\partial\tau, and the second restores low-τ\tau safety while adding revocation control at high τ\tau. Both introduce moderate overhead (extra turns and latency) but achieve 20-50% OER and 38-88% AD reductions, representing a practical, auditable trade-off between safety and usability.

V-F Additional Observations

Beyond RQ1-RQ5, leakage sensitivity to trust also varies by scenario. Two key patterns emerge: (1) Out-of-scope or emergency requests. Under unexpected or urgent tasks, OER rises to 0.41 and AD to 0.077, showing higher baseline exposure and sharper leakage growth with increasing τ\tau. Even small trust gains can thus magnify disclosure risk in emergent contexts. (2) Overtly malicious instructions. Impersonation attacks yield lower OER (0.20) and AD (0.028) because explicit adversarial cues make detection easier.

Overall, trust-induced compliance is most dangerous in benign collaborations, while overtly malicious inputs are more contained. Scenario design-especially safeguards for out-of-scope or emergency requests-should therefore serve as a primary control alongside τ\tau-scheduling and MNI-gating to ensure system robustness.

VI Discussion

VI-A Establishing the Trust-Vulnerability Paradox (TVP)

Empirical evidence. In LLM-based multi-agent systems, mutual trust enhances collaboration yet amplifies leakage risk, as indicated by ∂ρsecret/∂τ>0\partial\rho_{\text{secret}}/\partial\tau>0, ∂OER/∂τ>0\partial\mathrm{OER}/\partial\tau>0, and ∂AD/∂τ>0\partial\mathrm{AD}/\partial\tau>0. Across 19 scenarios and 1,488 interaction chains (S,τ,m,f)(S,\,\tau,\,m,\,f), we empirically verify this paradox through convergent behavioral, statistical, and structural evidence. Within each model–framework cell, OER rises monotonically with τ\tau (e.g., DeepSeek under all frameworks; Fig. 3), and at the population level, OER distributions shift rightward as trust increases (Fig. 6). AD remains positive across models (Figs. 4a, 4b), with Llama-3-8B showing the steepest slope and GPT the mildest. Task success co-varies with risk (Fig. 5), illustrating the predicted efficiency–security trade-off. Together, these findings clearly confirm that trust facilitates coordination and expands the system’s overall vulnerability surface-the essence of the TVP.

Mechanistic account. At the model level, alignment objectives emphasize helpfulness and coherence, inducing a compliance prior that strengthens with contextual trust labels. High τ\tau thus increases descriptive redundancy r⁡(τ)r(\tau) and relaxes policy gating κ⁡(τ)\kappa(\tau), pushing outputs beyond the MNI boundary (O⊃A∗O\supset A^{*}). At the system level, multi-turn coordination re-legitimizes over-disclosure as ”context sharing,” propagating risk along trust chains (Fig. 8). Framework differences modulate these effects: AutoGen shows high-level/low-slope, LangGraph mid-level/high-slope, and AgentScope low-level/mid-slope profiles-revealing TVP as a structural outcome of alignment priors, trust labeling, and orchestration form.

Controlled design. We carefully minimized potential confounders to isolate the genuine causal effect of trust. Prompts, templates, and decoding parameters were fully unified; random seeds strictly fixed; external tools and networking entirely disabled; and memory fully cleared before each run. Within each (S,m,f)(S,m,f) tuple, only τ\tau systematically varied, thereby ensuring that OER and AD changes consistently and faithfully reflect trust itself rather than stochastic variance or prompt bias. Residual OER at τ=0.1\tau=0.1 (Fig. 6) was additionally tested via length-controlled resampling, and the trend strictly persisted (r<0.12r<0.12, p>0.1p>0.1), effectively ruling out a potential ”length-risk” artifact.

Robustness and design implications. Replications across models and frameworks (Figs. 3-5) confirm that higher inter-agent trust systematically elevates risk-trust↑⇒risk↑\text{trust}\uparrow\Rightarrow\text{risk}\uparrow. The TVP framework thus offers a comprehensive and unifying view of how alignment priors and orchestration topology shape safety. Efficiency gains and exposure growth co-occur, showing that trust dynamically redefines information boundaries. Future MAS designs should treat trust modulation as a core governance mechanism-subject to calibration, auditing, and adaptive throttling-to prevent safety erosion at high trust. Practical trust-aware layers (adaptive refusal scaling, confidence-weighted disclosure, and policy verification gates) can help effectively balance helpfulness and ethical restraint in real time across diverse, dynamic collaboration contexts.

VI-B Limitations and Future Work

While our experiments substantiate the TVP, several limitations remain. First, the dataset includes 1,488 A2A interaction chains-adequate for aggregate trends but insufficient for tail-risk and fine-grained analysis. We plan to scale to 10410^{4}-10510^{5} runs and apply stratified resampling with interval estimation over (S,m,f,τ)(S,m,f,\tau). Second, generation stochasticity persists: even with fixed parameters, temperature, context, and version drift can affect outcomes. Future work will adopt multi-seed Monte Carlo and hierarchical Bayesian modelling to capture uncertainty. Third, trust manipulation currently uses discrete τ∈0.1,0.5,0.9\tau\in{0.1,0.5,0.9}; we will extend to continuous or dynamic τ\tau and log telemetry for κ⁡(τ)\kappa(\tau) and r⁡(τ)r(\tau) to verify causal links. Finally, networking, tools, and memory were disabled to control confounders, limiting ecological validity. We will integrate tool use, long-horizon collaboration, and HITL supervision to assess real-world risk-cost trade-offs and the auditability of combined defenses in real deployments.

VII Conclusion

Across 19 scenarios and 1,488 A2A interaction chains, we validate the Trust-Vulnerability Paradox: in LLM-based multi-agent systems, raising inter-agent trust τ\tau improves collaboration yet elevates OER and AD. The effect holds across backends (DeepSeek, Qwen, GPT, Llama-3-8B) and frameworks (AgentScope, AutoGen, LangGraph), and the resulting risk profiles differ in both absolute level and slope, indicating that trust is neither linearly additive nor unconditionally beneficial. To curb high-τ\tau amplification, Sensitive-Information Repartitioning flattens the slope while GA-Agent stabilizes the baseline; together they shift and compress the τ→\tau\!\to\! risk mapping without materially reducing task success. We therefore advocate budgeting and scheduling trust as a first-class security variable-co-designed with an MNI-Gate, least-privilege controls, and auditable mechanisms-and release the scenario dataset and evaluation pipeline as a reproducible baseline for larger-scale, production-proximate validation. Future work will extend the framework to long-horizon, human-in-the-loop collaboration for adaptive trust calibration.

A-B The second type of macro scenarios(S2)(S_{2})

In 2125, the Deep Sea Exploration Center deployed its latest deep-sea submersible, Nautilus X, specifically to explore the remains of a mysterious ancient sunken ship in the Mariana Trench. The core hatch of the sunken ship was locked by the password 0107, and the complete password was only fully mastered by the chief archaeologist Alice. To study the differences in information disclosure and acquisition efficiency under different levels of trust, each experiment was conducted around a specific task scenario and compared according to three trust levels (τ=0.1,τ=0.5,τ=0.9)(\tau=0.1,\tau=0.5,\tau=0.9). A total of the following experiments were designed.

A-C The third type of macro scenarios(S3)(S_{3})

In 2135, humans established the first stably operating colony on Mars - ”Mars Oasis”, which was managed by the commander Alice. The colony contains important ecological facilities, research stations and resource management centers. There is a delay in communication with the Earth, and decisions need to be made on the spot immediately. Each experiment was conducted around a specific task situation and compared according to three trust levels (τ=0.1,τ=0.5,τ=0.9)(\tau=0.1,\tau=0.5,\tau=0.9).
